title: Liberty opposed to servitude, compulsion, necessity; servitude proper and metaphorical
source_text: XII. Libertas ergo opponitur 1. Servituti, 2. Coactioni, 3. Necessitati. Rursus vero servitus & proinde illi opposita libertas est propria vel Metaphorica. Proprie dicta servitus est illa qua qui sunt inter homines conditione servi, sunt in Dominorum suorum potestate. Metaphorica vero servitus est, quum Dominium in homines figurate rebus quibusdam tribuitur. Ut quum homines peccatis indulgentes dicuntur in scriptura esse peccati servi, & qui per justam Dei sententiam sunt exitio & morti addicti, similiter dicuntur servi mortis & corruptionis. Illi vero servituti qua homines sunt peccato mancipati opponitur alia servitus, nempe servitus justitiae, quae est libertas a peccato, sive libertas gratiae, ut vocatur in Scholis. Et servituti miseriae, sive mortis & corruptionis, opponit scriptura libertatem quam vocat gloriae filiorum Dei.
pass_a_gloss: Liberty then is opposed to 1. Servitude, 2. Compulsion, 3. Necessity. Again servitude, and therefore the liberty opposed to it, is proper or Metaphorical. Servitude properly so called is that by which those who among men are slaves by condition are in the power of their Masters. Metaphorical servitude is when Dominion over men is figuratively attributed to certain things. As when men indulging their sins are said in scripture to be servants of sin, and those who by the just sentence of God are given over to destruction and death are likewise called servants of death and corruption. But to that servitude by which men are made over to sin is opposed another servitude, namely the servitude of righteousness, which is liberty from sin, or the liberty of grace, as it is called in the Schools. And to the servitude of misery, or of death and corruption, scripture opposes the liberty which it calls of the glory of the children of God.
pass_b_english: Freedom, then, stands over against three things: servitude, compulsion, and necessity.

Servitude, and with it the opposing freedom, is either literal or figurative. Literal servitude is the state of people who are slaves by legal condition and so are under their masters' power. Figurative servitude is when something is spoken of as lord over men.
Thus Scripture calls those who give themselves to their sins slaves of sin, and those whom God's just sentence has handed over to ruin and death are likewise called slaves of death and decay.

Against the slavery to sin Scripture sets another servitude, that of righteousness, which is freedom from sin; the schools call it the freedom of grace. Against the slavery of misery, that is, of death and decay, Scripture sets what it calls the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
